claim: The findings were measured on 2026-10-23 with agent-browser 0.39.1, the upstream linux-musl-x64 binary, sha256 `74507cdab98aa91bdc14346c545aff974640a225e43f8c3d6c23164f8c0f9bb9`, as pinned.
The browser used was Helium 0.18.1.1 (Chromium 154.0.8037.57, from nixpkgs) on NixOS.
Chrome for Testing could not be used because it doesn't start on NixOS (D-1).

Every run used the setup the spec prescribes: `--config` on every call, `HOME` set to a scratch folder, cwd a scratch folder, every `AGENT_BROWSER_*` removed, one profile per engine, Consent-O-Matic loaded except for Bing.
Two network exits were used and each capture says which.
The VPN exit was Proton, AS208172, Frankfurt; the controller's runs and the first half of the author's used it.
The residential exit was AS41110 DSLmobil, checked on ipinfo.io before every engine batch.

Ruling R3: `executablePath` is the first of `WEB_MCP_CHROME`; the newest Chrome for Testing if its `--version` starts (checked once per process; it does not on NixOS); `helium` on PATH; `chromium` on PATH.
Branded Chrome is never used as the search browser.
When no browser is found, the search fails naming `WEB_MCP_CHROME`.
The user agent carries the browser's own major version, reduced as Chrome does: `Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/<major>.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`.
On Windows the user agent has `Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64` in place of `X11; Linux x86_64`.
For Chrome for Testing the version comes from the folder name `chrome-<a.b.c.d>`, with no spawn.
For Helium, `helium --version` prints `Helium 0.18.1.1 (Chromium 154.0.8037.57)` and the major is the number after `Chromium `.
For Chromium, `chromium --version` prints `Chromium <a.b.c.d> …`.
Checked: httpbin.org/headers received exactly the configured `User-Agent`.
`agent-browser install` downloads Chrome for Testing into `<home>/.agent-browser/browsers/chrome-<full version>/`, flattening the zip's top folder.
`<home>` is `$HOME` on Linux and `%USERPROFILE%` on Windows.

The Chrome for Testing binary is `chrome-<ver>/chrome` on Linux or `chrome-<ver>\chrome.exe` on Windows; upstream also accepts `chrome-<ver>/chrome-linux64/chrome` and `chrome-<ver>\chrome-win64\chrome.exe`.
To find the newest Chrome for Testing: list `browsers/`, keep `chrome-<a>.<b>.<c>.<d>` entries whose binary exists, and take the highest by comparing the four numbers numerically.
Upstream sorts the folder names as strings (so `chrome-99.*` beats `chrome-156.*`); that must not be copied.

`agent-browser install` downloads Chrome for Testing even when a branded Chrome is installed (source, `install.rs:450-460`), and without `--executable-path` agent-browser prefers it over a system Chrome.
`agent-browser install` checks no hash of the Chrome for Testing zip.
On Windows upstream documents no location for Chrome for Testing; per the source it is `%USERPROFILE%\.agent-browser\browsers\chrome-<ver>\chrome.exe`.
Helium from nixpkgs dies 10 s after agent-browser launches it.
nixpkgs runs Helium inside `bwrap --die-with-parent`.
agent-browser launches the browser from a tokio blocking thread, which tokio retires after 10 s idle; `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` fires on that thread's exit and kills the browser.
agent-browser avoids `PDEATHSIG` itself for exactly this reason (comment in its `chrome.rs`, upstream issue #1157), but the bwrap wrapper brings it back.
Measured: the browser's processes vanish 10.0–10.5 s after `open`, every time, also inside one batch (`open`, `wait 12000`, `get url` answers `about:blank`).
After the browser dies, the next command silently launches a fresh browser on `about:blank`.
Helium started by hand from a shell stays up.
Consequence: a search whose batch crosses the 10 s mark loses its page.
Consequence: the profile is killed with SIGKILL, so cookies set in that window (consent answers) may never reach disk; a Google consent answered in one launch was asked again on the next.
Consequence: `idleTimeout` never matters for the browser while it dies at 10 s.

The fix that works is an `executablePath` that is a non-`exec` shell script (`#!/bin/sh` followed by `/home/<user>/.nix-profile/bin/helium "$@"`), so bwrap's parent is that shell, not the tokio thread.
With the wrapper the browser lived past 15 s, `close` still cleaned up everything in 0.4 s (agent-browser kills the process group), and no wrapper shell was left behind.
Everything from Step 4 on was measured with the wrapper.
Ruling R9: on Linux, web-mcp writes such a `#!/bin/sh` wrapper (no `exec`) beside the profile when the browser is helium, and uses it as `executablePath`.
nixpkgs' `chromium` is not bwrap-wrapped; this was not tested here because it isn't installed.
Helium is not plain Chromium: it loads three component extensions into every profile, uBlock Origin, `extstore-fixups` and the PDF viewer.
Bing still delivered its `li.b_ad` ads in the DOM under Helium (one of ten queries), so the parsers still see them.
Whether a built-in ad blocker fits "a normal user" is for the user to decide; nothing in the findings depends on it.
The Consent-O-Matic zip URL is `https://github.com/cavi-au/Consent-O-Matic/releases/download/v1.1.5/consent-o-matic-v1.1.5-unpacked-release-chromium.zip`.
The zip's sha256 is `37cec881fc5f53c84419e39d6a01cb79ff0b06b8df556219ac5c74887ba1473a` and it is 88,188 bytes; all match.

The zip's root layout is 17 regular files at the root, no folders, no symlinks: `manifest.json`, `service.js`, `content.js`, `content.css`, `ui.js`, `ui.css`, `editor.js`, `editor.html`, `options.html`, `popup.html`, `templates.html`, `main.css`, `hide.svg`, `minimize.svg`, `logo.svg`, `icon_48.png`, `icon_96.png`.
The extension is MV3, version 1.1.5, with permissions `activeTab`, `tabs`, `storage` and host `<all_urls>`.
The extension's defaults are `{A,B,D,E,F,X: false}`, meaning reject everything.
The extension's rules load from `raw.githubusercontent.com` at runtime.
Helium 154 loads the extension from `extensions` (registered as an unpacked command-line extension, service worker started), with extension id `ggheiilbfpnigmoiddealbmcjhffmpmg`.
On a fresh profile Consent-O-Matic opens `chrome-extension://…/options.html` in an extra tab, headless and headed alike; on the second launch of the same profile it doesn't.
agent-browser's `tab list` hides the onboarding tab (and the initial `chrome://newtab/`); only the CDP target list shows it.
`get url` and `get html` read agent-browser's own tab, the one `open` navigated.
The onboarding tab never got in the way, so nothing needs presetting for it.
A consent wall was seen only at Google, and only on its home page (`https://www.google.com/?hl=en`, VPN exit, German IP).
Google's search page was only ever seen as `/sorry` (on the VPN and on the rate-limited residential line), so a consent wall in front of `/search` was never observed.
Without the extension the Google consent wall stayed (30 s, two launches).
With the extension, Google redirects to `consent.google.com` and Consent-O-Matic answers "reject".
On a fresh profile the consent wall cleared after about 23 s, because the rule list is fetched first.
On a warm profile (rules cached, cookies cleared, 3 rounds) the consent wall cleared after 5.1–5.3 s, `open` included.
On a second launch there was no consent wall because the `SOCS` cookie persisted; with the 10 s kill it did not persist.
The fresh-profile consent time exceeds the 10 s engine deadline, so the first Google search on a new profile in the EU will read a consent page.
Recommendation: the ready expressions contain no consent marker, so the daemon keeps waiting while Consent-O-Matic clicks; a consent page read at the deadline still parses as `Blocked(Consent)`.
If Task 5 keeps "retry once", the retry has the warm-profile time of about 5 s.
Bing without the extension (R7) showed no consent wall on either network; `#bnp_container` was never present.
The fixture `google-consent.html` is the `consent.google.com` page from the home-page visit on the VPN.
`--config` replaces both auto-discovered config files.

With `--config` on the call, neither a planted `./agent-browser.json` (`{"headed": true}`) nor `~/.agent-browser/config.json` (`{"proxy": "http://127.0.0.1:9"}`) had any effect, alone or together: the browser ran `--headless=new` without `--proxy-server`, and httpbin answered.
Control without `--config`: the project file made the browser headed, and the user file added `--proxy-server` so the page failed with `ERR_PROXY_CONNECTION_FAILED`.
This contradicts the spec's amended sentence "`--config` does not keep `~/.agent-browser/config.json` out (it merges in)".
The controller's blank-page observation most likely came from a call without `--config`, which relaunches with the defaults anyway.
Scratch `HOME` and cwd (R5) stay harmless and keep agent-browser's own state out of the user's folders.
`args` is split on commas and newlines (controller); `--lang=en-US` alone is enough.
The `Accept-Language` seen by httpbin was `en-US,en;q=0.9`.
Every call carries `--config` (controller, R4): a call without it relaunches the default browser.
`close` followed at once by `open` fails 5 of 5 times: the `open` gets `Invalid response: EOF … outcome_unknown`, and an immediate retry gets `CDP WebSocket connect failed: Connection reset by peer`.
With a 1 s gap between `close` and `open`, 5 of 5 succeeded.
The session is gone about 0.1 s after `close` returns, when `<socket dir>/<session>.pid` and `.sock` disappear.
The socket dir is `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/agent-browser/` on Linux, overridable with `AGENT_BROWSER_SOCKET_DIR`.
An `open` right after the pid and sock files disappeared succeeded 3 of 3 times.
After a `close` (Windows' `close_after`, or a failed batch) the next search on that engine must wait for the pid and sock files to go (at most 1 s) or retry once.
Idle close: a session with `"idleTimeout": "120s"` left alone closed itself, daemon and browser, after 121.3–121.7 s.
After the idle close only `<session>.config` and `.target` stay in the socket dir.
`AGENT_BROWSER_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` is per call: the value the CLI call carries bounds that call's `wait`.
With the daemon started without `AGENT_BROWSER_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` and the call carrying 3000 / 8000, the wait timed out after 3000 / 8000 ms (the call took 4.0 / 8.9 s).
With the daemon started with `AGENT_BROWSER_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=3000` and the call without it, the timeout was 25000 ms, the default: the daemon's own environment is not used.
web-mcp sets `AGENT_BROWSER_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` on every call, as planned.
When the CLI is killed mid-`wait` (SIGTERM or SIGKILL, 1 s into a 20 s wait), the daemon finishes the wait first; the next command on that session answered 20.8 s later.
A killed search blocks its session for up to the timeout it was given, which web-mcp sets to the remaining time.
In a batch after a failed `wait`, without `--bail` the batch continues; `get html body` and `get url` both answered.
A failed batch entry is `{"success": false, "result": null}` and the output is still a JSON list.
Today's `batch_with` turns any failed entry into an error, so `render` must skip the `wait` entry, as planned.
`open` reports success on a blank page (controller); the outcome comes only from the parsed page.
A whole search batch on a running session took 0.3–2 s; the first in a session took 2–5 s, browser launch included.
Google's English URL parameters are `hl=en&gl=us&num=10`, unverified because its result page was not seen.
Bing's English URL parameters are `setlang=en-US&cc=US`, giving an English page with no consent wall.
DuckDuckGo's English URL parameters are `kl=us-en&ia=web`; the page shows "US (English)".
Brave's English URL parameters are `source=web&lang=en`; `lang` is Brave's language parameter.
Scholar's English URL parameter is `hl=en`, giving an English page.
Semantic Scholar's URL parameter is `sort=relevance`, unverified because its result page was not seen.
Bing, DuckDuckGo, Brave and Scholar's settings were checked on their live result pages.
`sort=relevance` is not a language setting: Semantic Scholar has no language parameter in its URL, and its page was never seen past the challenge.
Brave with `&lang=de` turned the page German (`<html lang="de-de">`, tabs "Fragen, Alles, Bilder…"); `ui_lang` and `country` changed nothing visible.
Without `lang`, Brave's page was already English, from `Accept-Language`.
`headed` is `false` for all six engines.
Brave, Scholar, Bing and DuckDuckGo never reached 3 blocks in 10 queries.
Google and Semantic Scholar were blocked 10 of 10 both headless and headed, but only after the line had been flagged, so the headed repeat says nothing about headed versus headless.

Step 6 ran ten queries per engine as the product runs them: one batch per query (`open`, `wait --fn <ready>`, `get html body`, `get url`), `AGENT_BROWSER_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=10000`, queries about 1 s apart, a persistent profile per engine (fresh for the residential run).
Brave: 10/10 results residential headless (0.8–2.0 s); headed not needed; results on the VPN.
Scholar: 10/10 results residential headless (0.3–2.0 s); headed not needed; results on the VPN.
Bing: 10/10 results residential headless (0.3–3.1 s); headed not needed; on the VPN the controller got an empty page and the author got results.
DuckDuckGo: 9/10 results residential headless with a CAPTCHA on the 10th; headed not needed; on the VPN the controller got an error-lite page and the author got results.
Google: 10/10 `/sorry` residential headless (IP already flagged), 10/10 `/sorry` residential headed (flagged), and `/sorry` CAPTCHA on the VPN.
Semantic Scholar: 10/10 "Human Verification" residential headless, 10/10 headed, and "Human Verification" on the VPN.
Google is rate-limited on the residential line, not blocked outright: the user watched it show results on the first try, and `/sorry` came only after many requests in a row.

The author's Google counts were taken after that burst from an IP Google had already flagged: even the first residential request on a fresh profile got `/sorry`, and at about 20:45 the controller got `/sorry` on a fresh profile with consent already cleared; so the 10/10 measures the flag, not this browser.
Semantic Scholar answered every request on both networks, headless and headed, with its "Human Verification" challenge; no request ever reached a result page.
The burst caveat may also apply to Semantic Scholar: all residential requests came within minutes, about 1 s apart.
Per R8 the Google and Semantic Scholar result-page parsers are written from current markup and their fixture tests are ignored until a result page is captured.
Live runs must space their queries like a person (seconds to minutes apart, not about 1 s), or they measure their own rate limit.
DuckDuckGo's CAPTCHA (`anomaly-modal`) came on the 10th query after about 10 s of back-to-back searching; the product doesn't search that fast, but the marker is real.

Bing and DuckDuckGo answered on the author's VPN runs (a Proton Frankfurt exit) but not on the controller's; the author's runs had the bwrap fix and perhaps a different exit, and the two were not separated.
Each ready expression has the form `!!(document.body && (results || no-results || block))`.
"Checked" means the part matched its committed fixture (loaded into a blank page) and the live page in Step 6; "unverified" parts come from markup the author knows, not from a capture.

Google: results `#rso a h3, #search a h3` (unverified); no-results "did not match any documents" in `#topstuff, #botstuff, #rcnt` (unverified); block is the `/sorry` path or `#captcha-form, form[action="index"] #recaptcha` (checked).

Bing: results `#b_results > li.b_algo` and no-results `#b_results > li.b_no` (both checked); block is the `/challenge` path or `#b_captcha, iframe[src*="captcha"], iframe[src*="challenges.cloudflare.com"]` (unverified).

DuckDuckGo: all three parts checked: results `article[data-testid="result"]`; no-results "No results found for" in a `[data-testid="mainline"]` section; block `a[href^="mailto:error-lite"], .anomaly-modal__title` (the anomaly modal and the html endpoint's error-lite page).
Brave: results `.snippet[data-type="web"]` (checked); no-results `/No results found|Not many great matches/` in `#results, main` and block are unverified because Brave never showed either.
Brave's block marker is DOM only, `#captcha, form[action*="captcha"]`, with no title or path test, because Brave puts the query in the title (R14).

Scholar: results `#gs_res_ccl_mid .gs_r.gs_or .gs_ri` and no-results "did not match any articles" in `#gs_res_ccl_top` (both checked); block is the `/sorry` path or `#gs_captcha_ccl, #captcha-form, #recaptcha` (unverified).

Semantic Scholar: block checked for both challenge stages (`#captcha-container, #challenge-container` or `document.title === 'Human Verification'`); results `[data-test-id="search-result"], .cl-paper-row` and no-results `/No results|could not find any|couldn.t find any/i` in `[data-test-id="search-results"], main` are unverified.

Semantic Scholar's challenge has two stages: first a 772-byte noscript page ("we need to verify that you're not a robot"), then the rendered AWS WAF page ("Let's confirm you are human", `#captcha-container`).
The Semantic Scholar ready expression fires on the first challenge stage, so the parser must call both stages `Captcha`.
Once, on the VPN, `get html body` failed with `Element not found: body` during the Semantic Scholar challenge; the next read worked.
Scholar's page always carries a hidden "The system can't perform the operation now" div, which is not a block marker.
Brave answers nonsense queries with relaxed results ("search operators were not applied", "Too few matches"), never with an empty page (5 tries).
Google's `/sorry` page is English with `hl=en`; its marker is `form#captcha-form` holding `div#recaptcha`.
The fixtures live in `crates/web-mcp/tests/fixtures/engines/`, each being the `get html body` of the page.
Script bodies were dropped in the two Bing fixture files, which are still about 300 KB.
In `google-captcha.html` the client IP (now `0.0.0.0`), the `q` token that encodes it, `sei` and the reCAPTCHA `data-s`/`s=` tokens (now `DUMMY`) were scrubbed.
In `google-consent.html` the `escs` token (now `DUMMY`) and the account sign-in URLs (now `#`) were scrubbed.
In `bing.html` the located place and coordinates were scrubbed (`data-lat="0"`, `data-lon="0"`, empty `data-disp`).
No parser marker lives in any of the scrubbed values.
`brave.html`: residential, query `tokio select cancellation safety`, 20 web results.
`scholar.html`: residential, query `retrieval augmented generation`, 10 results.
`scholar-none.html`: VPN, quoted nonsense query, "did not match any articles".
`bing.html`: residential, query `tokio select cancellation safety`, 10 results.
`bing-ads.html`: residential, query `postgres partial index example`, with `li.b_ad` ads.
`bing-none.html`: residential, nonsense query, `li.b_no` "There are no results for".
`duckduckgo.html`: residential, query `tokio select cancellation safety`, 10 results.
`duckduckgo-none.html`: VPN, quoted nonsense query, "No results found for".
`duckduckgo-captcha.html`: residential, anomaly modal ("bots use DuckDuckGo too").
`duckduckgo-captcha-lite.html`: VPN, html.duckduckgo.com error-lite page from the controller's run.
`google-captcha.html`: residential, `/sorry` "unusual traffic" reCAPTCHA page.
`google-consent.html`: VPN, `consent.google.com` reached from the home page.
`semanticscholar-captcha.html`: residential, AWS WAF "Let's confirm you are human".
`semanticscholar-captcha-noscript.html`: residential, the challenge's first, noscript stage.
For fixtures not obtained, their Task 2 tests are dropped or ignored per R8, and the case falls to `Unrecognised`.
`google.html` and `google-none.html` were not obtained: `/sorry` on the VPN, and on the residential line only after it was flagged (rate limit, see Step 6).
`semanticscholar.html` and `semanticscholar-none.html` were not obtained: the challenge came on every request on both networks (burst caveat).
`brave-none.html` was not obtained because Brave never shows an empty result page.
`bing-captcha.html`, `brave-captcha.html` and `scholar-captcha.html` were not obtained because those engines were never blocked.
Bing's empty page on the controller's VPN run had no markup (1 byte), so it is no fixture.
`bing-consent.html` and any consent page in front of a search were never seen.
